flashcards.front: What is the primary threat vector for Asymmetric Cryptography?
flashcards.back_definition: Adversaries exploit unvalidated self-signed certificates on TLS public keys to bypass standard perimeter security controls.
flashcards.back_example: Example: TLS Fail: CN name mismatch (g00gle.com CN presented on utility.com)
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse this threat with other layers (like physical breaches or certificate revocations) which target different assets.
flashcards.back_hook: Recall: unvalidated self-signed certificates is the unlocked door; TLS public keys is what the attacker wants to steal.

flashcards.front: How does the security team mitigate Asymmetric Cryptography threats?
flashcards.back_definition: Deploying and enforcing Root CA public key infrastructure validation directly hardens TLS public keys and blocks unauthorized connections.
flashcards.back_example: Action: Update security configurations to require Root CA public key infrastructure validation.
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse mitigation (actively blocking the exploit) with detection (simply logging or alerting the event).
flashcards.back_hook: Mitigation is the shield; detection is the security camera.

flashcards.front: How do analysts detect exploitation of Asymmetric Cryptography?
flashcards.back_definition: By auditing event data and implementing logic flags built to alert on OCSP revocation status queries.
flashcards.back_example: Syslog trace: TLS Fail: CN name mismatch (g00gle.com CN presented on utility.com)
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse signature-based detection (matching known strings) with anomaly-based detection (mapping dynamic standard deviations).
flashcards.back_hook: Detection is looking for the fingerprint left behind by the threat.
